newsitem.title: UK: British forces escape injury in IRA bomb attack.
newsitem.headline: British forces escape injury in IRA bomb attack.

text.p: IRA guerrillas set off a bomb as British forces patrolled an Irish nationalist zone in West Belfast on Thursday, but no one was seriously hurt, police said.

The device exploded behind a garden wall seconds after soldiers and police had passed along a road in the sprawling Ballymurphy housing estate. Several arrests were made in a follow-up security operation.
Police sources said security personnel and civilians were treated for shock after the blast scattered debris across the narrow street and shook houses.

Irish Republican Army guerrillas, fighting to end British rule over Northern Ireland, displayed total disregard for residents and security forces alike, police Chief Inspector Graham Shields said at the scene.

"We are very fortunate that we don't have anybody very seriously injured or killed. It is a densely populated built-up area with lots of children about. It shows the contempt that the IRA hold the people of Ballymurphy in, as well as the security forces, whenever they undertake such a reckless act."
IRA guerrillas, who abandoned a 17-month truce in February 1996, have launched frequent attacks on security forces in the province since Christmas.

Two British soldiers have been killed in bomb and gun attacks since October in a campaign that wrecked an attempted peace process and rattled a truce operated by pro-British Loyalist guerrillas for more than two years.

Britain says Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, will not be given a seat in peace talks until it abandons violence. Talks on the province's future were adjourned on Wednesday until June ahead of the British election, expected in May.

A pro-British politician blamed Protestant guerrillas on Thursday for a bomb near a Sinn Fein office in Monaghan town in the Irish Republic last Monday but said it did not mark the end of the Loyalist truce. The device failed to explode.

David Ervine, a leader of the political arm of the banned Loyalist Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF), said he had not ascertained which group left the device but added: "I am fairly certain in my own mind that it was the work of Loyalism."

Irish police confirmed the 12 kg (25 lb) bomb contained commercial explosive that security analysts say was used in UVF bombs before the illegal Combined Loyalist Military Command called a truce in October 1994.
The CLMC groups the UVF and three other outlawed groups that killed Irish nationalists in retaliation for the IRA's campaign to merge the largely Protestant region with Catholic Ireland.
